pretest.text: What generally makes a password stronger?

choices.text: Adding a symbol like "!" at the end
Being long and unique
Being easy to say out loud
Using your birth year

pretest.explanation: Length and uniqueness matter far more than a single substituted symbol.

pretest.text: Is it safe to reuse the same password across multiple accounts?

choices.text: No — one breach can expose every account that reused it
Yes, if the accounts are unrelated
Only for unimportant accounts
Yes, as long as it is long

pretest.explanation: Reusing a password means a single leak can be tried against every other account using it.

pretest.text: What does multi-factor authentication (MFA) add?

choices.text: Faster login times
Unlimited password resets
A stronger password automatically
A second layer of proof beyond your password

pretest.explanation: MFA requires a second factor — like a code on your phone — so a stolen password alone is not enough to log in.

pretest.text: What is "credential stuffing"?

choices.text: A way to recover a forgotten password
Guessing passwords one character at a time
Trying leaked username/password pairs against other sites
A type of firewall

pretest.explanation: Credential stuffing automates trying passwords leaked from one breach against many other services.

pretest.text: What should you do first if a service you use reports a data breach?

choices.text: Nothing, breaches are common
Change your password for that service right away
Delete the account without changing anything
Wait a few months

pretest.explanation: Changing the password immediately limits how long a possibly-leaked credential stays useful to an attacker.

pretest.text: Why is a multi-word passphrase like "sunset-coffee-bridge-winter" strong against brute-force attacks?

choices.text: Its substantial length creates exponentially more combinations for attackers to test
It requires an internet connection to decrypt
It expires automatically after 30 days
It uses dictionary words that are easy to guess

pretest.explanation: Length provides exponential combinatorial strength against automated password-cracking software.

pretest.text: Why is using an authenticator app generally more secure than receiving 2FA codes via SMS text message?

choices.text: SMS text messages cost money to send
Authenticator apps can only be used on computers
Authenticator apps do not need phone batteries
SMS messages can be intercepted or stolen through SIM swapping attacks

pretest.explanation: SMS-based 2FA is susceptible to SIM-swapping and carrier interception, whereas app-based TOTP tokens remain stored securely on your device.

pretest.text: What is the main security advantage of using a reputable password manager?

choices.text: It prevents all phishing websites automatically
It allows you to use one simple password everywhere
It generates and securely stores unique, complex passwords for every single service
It eliminates the need for two-factor authentication

pretest.explanation: Password managers solve password reuse by creating and remembering distinct, high-entropy passwords for all your accounts.

quiz.text: Which of the following is the strongest password?

choices.text: password123
Tr0ub4dor&3
correct-horse-battery-staple-42
P@ssw0rd

quiz.explanation: Length and unpredictability matter more than symbol substitution — a long passphrase is harder to crack than a short, "complex" password.

quiz.text: What is credential stuffing?

choices.text: Reusing leaked username/password pairs against other sites
Guessing a password one character at a time
A type of phishing email
A password recovery technique

quiz.explanation: Credential stuffing automates trying leaked credentials from one breach against many other services, exploiting password reuse.

quiz.text: Why should you enable multi-factor authentication (MFA)?

choices.text: It replaces the need for a password
It blocks all phishing emails
It adds a second layer of protection beyond your password
It automatically generates strong passwords

quiz.explanation: MFA requires a second factor — like a code or approval on another device — so a stolen password alone is not enough to log in.

quiz.text: What should you do first if a service you use reports a data breach?

choices.text: Wait to see if you are affected before doing anything
Change your password for that service immediately
Delete your account without changing anything
Ignore it since breaches are common

quiz.explanation: Changing the password right away limits how long a potentially leaked credential remains useful to an attacker.

quiz.text: What makes a passphrase like 'correct horse battery staple' strong?

choices.text: It uses special characters
It is short and easy to type
It is long and hard to guess despite being memorable
It is based on a single dictionary word

quiz.explanation: Length is the dominant factor in resisting brute-force attacks, and a memorable passphrase avoids the temptation to write it down or reuse it.

quiz.text: Why is using an authenticator app (TOTP) safer than receiving 2FA codes via SMS?

choices.text: SMS codes expire too quickly to type
SMS can be intercepted through SIM swapping or mobile network spoofing
Authenticator apps automatically change your password every hour
SMS messages are blocked by all web browsers

quiz.explanation: SIM-swap fraud allows criminals to redirect your SMS messages to their own device, bypassing text-based 2FA.

quiz.text: What is the primary role of a master password in a password manager?

choices.text: It is sent to every website you log into
It is the single strong key used locally to encrypt and unlock your entire password vault
It allows tech support to access your accounts if you forget your details
It disables the need for device encryption

quiz.explanation: A strong master password encrypts your password database so that only you can decrypt the stored credentials.

quiz.text: What physical security threat involves someone looking over your shoulder to see you type your PIN or password?

choices.text: Shoulder surfing
Dumpster diving
Tailgating
Watering hole attack

quiz.explanation: Shoulder surfing is a direct observation technique used by attackers in public or crowded areas to steal credentials.

quiz.text: If you discover one of your accounts was breached, why must you also change passwords on other accounts that shared that password?

choices.text: Breached companies automatically notify all other websites
Automated credential stuffing bots will try the exposed password across hundreds of popular services
Your internet connection will be suspended otherwise
Password hashing algorithms expire after a breach

quiz.explanation: Attackers immediately run leaked email/password pairs through credential stuffing scripts against other platforms.

quiz.text: Which factor represents "something you are" in Multi-Factor Authentication?

choices.text: A physical hardware security key (FIDO token)
A fingerprint or facial biometric scan
A PIN number known only to you
An SMS verification code

quiz.explanation: Biometrics (fingerprints, facial recognition, iris scans) represent the "inherence" factor ("something you are").

pretest.text: What is phishing?

choices.text: A firewall misconfiguration
A fraudulent attempt to trick someone into revealing sensitive information
A type of antivirus scan
A slow internet connection

pretest.explanation: Phishing impersonates a trusted sender to trick you into giving up credentials or clicking a malicious link.

pretest.text: Which is a common red flag in a phishing email?

choices.text: A short subject line
A company logo
A greeting with your name
A sender address that does not match the real company

pretest.explanation: A mismatched sender address is one of the most reliable signs of a spoofed email.

pretest.text: Is it safe to click a link in an urgent "verify your account now" email?

choices.text: Yes, if the email looks professional
Only if it has your name in it
Yes, urgency means it is important
No — verify through a separately-trusted channel first

pretest.explanation: Urgency is a manipulation tactic — verifying through a channel you already trust is much safer.

pretest.text: What should you do with an unexpected attachment from an unknown sender?

choices.text: Save it for later
Open it to see what it is
Avoid opening it and report it
Forward it to a coworker first

pretest.explanation: Reporting an unopened suspicious attachment protects you and anyone else who received the same email.

pretest.text: Why do phishing emails often create a sense of urgency?

choices.text: It is required by email providers
To pressure you into acting before you think it through
To make the email load faster
It has no real purpose

pretest.explanation: Urgency pushes victims to act quickly, before they can carefully evaluate the request.

pretest.text: What distinguishes "spear phishing" from ordinary mass phishing emails?

choices.text: Spear phishing is tailored with specific personal or organizational details to deceive a targeted individual
Spear phishing never contains links or attachments
Spear phishing is sent exclusively through physical postal mail
Spear phishing only targets government agencies

pretest.explanation: Spear phishing leverages researched personal or job-related information to make fraudulent communications appear genuine.

pretest.text: How can you safely inspect the true destination of a hyperlink in an email before clicking it?

choices.text: Right-click and bookmark the link
Reply to the sender asking where it leads
Click it and quickly close the browser tab
Hover your cursor over the link to preview the actual destination URL in the status bar or tooltip

pretest.explanation: Hovering allows you to inspect the real destination domain without triggering any network requests to the target server.

pretest.text: Which attachment file extension typically presents the highest immediate risk of executing malware?

choices.text: An audio file (.mp3)
A plain text file (.txt)
An executable or macro script file (.exe, .scr, or .vbs)
An image file (.png)

pretest.explanation: Executable binaries and script extensions can directly run malicious instructions on your operating system upon opening.

quiz.text: What is the safest way to verify a suspicious payment request email?

choices.text: Reply to the email asking for confirmation
Call the vendor using a known, trusted phone number
Click the link to see where it leads
Forward it to a coworker for their opinion

quiz.explanation: Verifying through a channel you already trust — not the email itself — confirms whether the request is real.

quiz.text: Which of these is a common sign of a phishing email?

choices.text: A sender address that does not match the real company
A professional-looking logo
Correct spelling and grammar
An email signature

quiz.explanation: Mismatched sender domains are one of the most reliable signs of a spoofed or phishing email.

quiz.text: What should you do with an unexpected attachment from an unknown sender?

choices.text: Open it to see what it is
Avoid opening it and report it
Forward it to IT after opening
Save it for later

quiz.explanation: Reporting an unopened suspicious attachment protects both you and anyone else who may have received the same email.

quiz.text: What is a fake login page designed to do?

choices.text: Speed up your login
Steal your entered credentials
Save your password securely
Verify your identity

quiz.explanation: A convincing lookalike login page exists solely to capture whatever credentials are typed into it.

quiz.text: Why is verifying through a known channel better than replying to a suspicious email?

choices.text: It is faster
It confirms you are talking to the real organization, not the attacker
It is required by law
It automatically blocks the sender

quiz.explanation: Replying only keeps the conversation with whoever sent the email — which may be the attacker. A known channel bypasses them entirely.

quiz.text: What is "spear phishing"?

choices.text: Phishing emails broadcast randomly to millions of inboxes
Highly tailored attacks targeting a specific individual using customized background information
A denial-of-service attack targeting email servers
A hardware attack carried out through Ethernet cables

quiz.explanation: Spear phishing targets specific individuals or roles using research gathered about the victim to increase credibility.

quiz.text: In the URL "https://login.microsoft.com.account-verify-365.net/auth", what is the actual domain hosting the page?

choices.text: microsoft.com
login.microsoft.com
account-verify-365.net
auth.net

quiz.explanation: The domain immediately preceding the top-level domain and first single slash is the true host: account-verify-365.net.

quiz.text: What is "smishing"?

choices.text: Phishing attacks conducted via SMS text messages
Malicious ads displayed inside social media apps
Phishing conducted entirely through voice phone calls
Eavesdropping on public Bluetooth connections

quiz.explanation: Smishing (SMS phishing) sends deceptive text messages with malicious links or urgent demands to mobile users.

quiz.text: Why do malicious Word or Excel attachments often prompt users to "Enable Macros" or "Enable Content"?

choices.text: To decrypt the document font files
To execute embedded automated script code that downloads and installs malware
To verify the reader has an active Office license
To connect the document to cloud storage

quiz.explanation: Macros are programs embedded in documents; enabling them allows malicious scripts to download and execute payloads.

quiz.text: What should you do immediately if you realize you entered your corporate password into a fake login page?

choices.text: Wait to see if unauthorized logins occur over the weekend
Immediately change your password and report the incident to your security/IT team
Delete your browser history and restart your device
Send an angry reply to the phishing email

quiz.explanation: Immediate password changes and prompt reporting enable the security team to revoke active sessions and contain compromise.

pretest.text: What is malware?

choices.text: Software that speeds up your computer
Malicious software designed to damage, steal, or hold data hostage
A built-in Windows tool
A type of web browser

pretest.explanation: Malware is a broad category covering viruses, ransomware, trojans, and spyware.

pretest.text: What is ransomware?

choices.text: A discount coupon scam
Free antivirus software
A password manager
Malware that locks your files and demands payment

pretest.explanation: Ransomware encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the (unguaranteed) key to unlock them.

pretest.text: Is downloading free software from an unofficial website risky?

choices.text: Only on old computers
Only if you have no antivirus
No, free is always safe
Yes — it is often bundled with malware

pretest.explanation: Unofficial download sources frequently bundle malicious software alongside the free tool being offered.

pretest.text: What is one of the best defenses against malware?

choices.text: Using the same password everywhere
Never restarting your computer
Keeping your software and operating system updated
Disabling your internet permanently

pretest.explanation: Updates close the security holes that malware relies on to spread.

pretest.text: What should you do if you find an unknown USB drive?

choices.text: Plug it in to see who owns it
Give it to IT without plugging it in
Use it for personal storage
Format it immediately yourself

pretest.explanation: Unknown USB drives are a known malware delivery method — IT can inspect them safely.

pretest.text: What is spyware designed to do without the computer owner's knowledge?

choices.text: Quietly monitor keystrokes, browsing habits, and credentials to send to an attacker
Display harmless desktop wallpaper notifications
Optimize operating system battery health
Speed up hard drive performance

pretest.explanation: Spyware stealthily tracks sensitive user inputs, web sessions, and saved passwords to exfiltrate to malicious operators.

pretest.text: Why is applying operating system and software security patches promptly so critical?

choices.text: Software companies disable devices that miss an update
Patches clean all temporary browser cookies
Patches always add new graphical themes
Patches fix discovered security flaws before attackers can exploit them

pretest.explanation: Unpatched software leaves known security holes open to exploitation by automated malware tools.

pretest.text: Why are isolated, offline backups essential for recovering from a ransomware infection?

choices.text: Offline backups delete the virus automatically
Offline backups load web pages faster
Ransomware cannot reach or encrypt storage media physically disconnected from the network
Cloud backups are always corrupted by firewalls

pretest.explanation: An offline (air-gapped) backup guarantees a clean, unencrypted copy of your critical data that the malware could not access.

quiz.text: Why are free downloads from unofficial websites risky?

choices.text: They are always slower
They are often bundled with malware
They cost more later
They require an account

quiz.explanation: Unofficial download sources frequently bundle malicious software alongside the free tool being offered.

quiz.text: What should you do if you find an unknown USB drive?

choices.text: Plug it in to see who owns it
Give it to IT without plugging it in
Use it for personal storage
Throw it away immediately

quiz.explanation: Unknown USB drives are a known malware delivery method — IT can safely inspect them without exposing your device.

quiz.text: What is ransomware?

choices.text: Software that speeds up your computer
Malware that locks your files and demands payment
A type of antivirus
A firewall setting

quiz.explanation: Ransomware encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the (unguaranteed) key to unlock them.

quiz.text: What is the recommended response to a ransomware pop-up?

choices.text: Pay immediately to avoid losing files
Disconnect from the network and contact IT
Restart the computer repeatedly
Ignore it and keep working

quiz.explanation: Disconnecting limits further spread while IT investigates and restores from backup.

quiz.text: Why doesn't paying a ransomware demand guarantee your files back?

choices.text: Attackers are legally required to unlock files
There is no guarantee the attacker will restore access after payment
Payment is always refunded
Ransomware deletes files instead of encrypting them

quiz.explanation: Paying funds the attacker with no enforceable guarantee that access will actually be restored.

quiz.text: What is a "Trojan" in computer security?

choices.text: Malware disguised as legitimate or useful software to trick users into running it
A hardware device that intercepts wireless signals
A security patch released by an operating system vendor
An antivirus program that has expired

quiz.explanation: A Trojan conceals its malicious payload inside what appears to be a normal utility, game, or document.

quiz.text: What type of malware silently records every keystroke typed on a keyboard to capture passwords and card numbers?

choices.text: Keylogger
Adware
Defragmenter
Boot sector scanner

quiz.explanation: Keyloggers capture hardware keystrokes and software inputs, transmitting credentials directly to cybercriminals.

quiz.text: Why is enabling automatic software updates strongly recommended for operating systems and browsers?

choices.text: It speeds up device battery charging times
It patches known vulnerabilities before automated exploit kits can weaponize them against your device
It prevents all spam emails from reaching your inbox
It clears device physical memory on startup

quiz.explanation: Attackers scan for unpatched software; automatic updates ensure security vulnerabilities are fixed as soon as patches exist.

quiz.text: Why is maintaining an offline ("air-gapped") backup crucial for recovering from modern ransomware attacks?

choices.text: Offline backups process data faster than cloud backups
Ransomware cannot reach or encrypt storage drives that are physically disconnected from the network
Cloud storage providers delete backups after three days
Offline backups prevent hardware overheating

quiz.explanation: Modern ransomware actively searches network shares and connected drives to encrypt backups; offline media remains immune.

quiz.text: Why is disabling the "AutoRun" or "AutoPlay" feature on operating systems a sound security defense?

choices.text: It stops USB drives from running potentially malicious programs automatically upon insertion
It saves battery power when playing music
It prevents flash drives from running out of storage
It makes copying files three times faster

quiz.explanation: Disabling AutoRun ensures code on removable media cannot execute without explicit user confirmation.

pretest.text: Does seeing "HTTPS" and a padlock mean a website is completely safe?

choices.text: Yes, always
No — it only means the connection is encrypted, not that the site is trustworthy
It means the site is government-approved
It means the site has no ads

pretest.explanation: HTTPS encrypts the connection, but attackers can obtain valid certificates for malicious sites too.

pretest.text: Is public Wi-Fi safe for logging into sensitive accounts without protection?

choices.text: No — traffic can potentially be intercepted by others on the network
Only at coffee shops
Only if the network has a password
Yes, always

pretest.explanation: Open or shared networks make it easier for others on the same Wi-Fi to intercept unencrypted traffic.

pretest.text: What is a common warning sign of a scam shopping website?

choices.text: Product photos
A working search bar
Extreme discounts like 90% off on an unfamiliar site
A visible contact page

pretest.text: What should you do about an unexpected "your browser is out of date" pop-up with a download button?

choices.text: Ignore it, it will go away in a week
Click it immediately to stay safe
Avoid clicking it — it is a common malware trick
Restart your computer instead

pretest.explanation: Fake update pop-ups are a common way to trick visitors into downloading malware.

pretest.text: What helps protect sensitive logins while using public Wi-Fi?

choices.text: A VPN or a trusted, private network
A stronger Wi-Fi password only
Using an older browser
Disabling your antivirus

pretest.explanation: A VPN or trusted network protects sensitive traffic from others who may share the same public Wi-Fi.

pretest.text: What does a browser certificate error such as "Your connection is not private" typically warn you about?

choices.text: The web server identity cannot be verified or the connection might be intercepted
The website has too many animated images
Your home Wi-Fi router is turned off
Your monitor display resolution is too low

pretest.explanation: Certificate errors indicate potential man-in-the-middle attacks, invalid encryption, or expired domain credentials.

pretest.text: What is "typosquatting" (URL hijacking)?

choices.text: Purchasing domain names for non-profit organizations
A tool used by web designers to test typography
Registering misspelled variants of popular domain names to mislead visitors to fake sites
Typing a search query too quickly in a search engine

pretest.explanation: Attackers register common spelling errors of popular sites (e.g., paypa1.com or examp1e.com) to catch accidental mistypes.

pretest.text: Why should you avoid accessing sensitive accounts on open, password-free public Wi-Fi hotspots without a VPN?

choices.text: Search engines block all searches on public Wi-Fi
Public Wi-Fi networks disconnect every five minutes
Unencrypted local network traffic can be monitored or spoofed by other devices on the same access point
Public Wi-Fi charges hidden fees per website visited

pretest.explanation: Open access points allow malicious peers on the same wireless network to analyze broadcast packets or launch spoofing attacks.

quiz.text: Why is public Wi-Fi risky for sensitive logins?

choices.text: It is usually slower
Traffic can potentially be intercepted by others on the network
It costs more data
It blocks secure websites

quiz.explanation: Open networks let others sharing the same Wi-Fi potentially intercept unencrypted traffic.

quiz.text: What should you do before entering payment details on an unfamiliar site?

choices.text: Trust it if the discount is large
Check reviews and the site's reputation first
Enter details quickly before the deal ends
Ask a friend to enter it for you

quiz.explanation: A quick reputation check can reveal a scam site before any payment details are entered.

quiz.text: What is a warning sign of a scam shopping site?

choices.text: Extreme discounts like 90% off on an unfamiliar site
A working contact page
HTTPS in the address bar
Product photos

quiz.explanation: Unrealistic discounts on unfamiliar sites are a common tactic used to harvest payment details.

quiz.text: Why should you be cautious about browser extensions demanded by a random website?

choices.text: They always slow down your browser
They can be a way to deliver malware
They are always free
They require a restart

quiz.explanation: Extensions demanded by an unrelated site are a common malware delivery method disguised as a requirement.

quiz.text: What is the safest way to access a sensitive account like banking?

choices.text: Any public Wi-Fi network
A trusted network or a VPN
Any browser extension that promises security
A shared computer

quiz.explanation: A trusted network or VPN protects sensitive traffic from others who may share the same public Wi-Fi.

quiz.text: What is 'typosquatting' (also known as URL hijacking)?

choices.text: Registering misspelled domain names of popular sites to deceive visitors
A tool that automatically corrects typing errors in search queries
A browser extension that compresses website source code
A technique that boosts download speeds across networks

quiz.explanation: Typosquatters register misspelled variants of familiar websites to trick users into visiting phishing or malware-hosting pages.

quiz.text: Does a padlock icon (HTTPS) next to a URL mean the website is completely trustworthy?

choices.text: Yes, malicious actors and scam websites are strictly barred from getting SSL certificates
No, HTTPS only encrypts the connection; malicious and scam websites can also have HTTPS
Yes, but only when accessed from desktop computers

quiz.explanation: HTTPS ensures communication between your device and the website is encrypted, but scam and phishing websites can also acquire valid SSL certificates.

quiz.text: When your browser displays a full-page red warning stating 'Your connection is not private' (SSL/TLS certificate error), what should you do?

choices.text: Ignore the alert and proceed immediately to log in
Do not bypass the warning or submit confidential data on that connection
Turn off your device antivirus software and refresh
Disable your firewall permanently

quiz.explanation: A certificate mismatch or error can signal an insecure connection or man-in-the-middle attack; you should avoid sending personal data.

quiz.text: If an urgent browser pop-up freezes your screen claiming 'VIRUS DETECTED! CALL TECH SUPPORT NOW', what is the safest action?

choices.text: Call the helpline number shown on the screen immediately
Close the tab or browser process via Task Manager and avoid calling the number
Download the cleanup software linked in the pop-up
Provide your remote desktop credentials so they can inspect your computer

quiz.explanation: Legitimate operating systems do not display browser pop-ups demanding you call a phone number. These are tech-support scam pages designed to gain remote access.

quiz.text: What does 'Incognito' or 'Private Browsing' mode actually do?

It prevents your local browser from saving browsing history, cookies, and form data after closing the session
It acts as an impenetrable VPN that conceals your real physical location
It automatically cleanses downloaded files of all viruses and malware

quiz.explanation: Private browsing only keeps your local device from recording session history and cookies; school/work networks and visited websites can still observe your traffic.

pretest.text: What is data privacy primarily concerned with?

choices.text: Making apps load faster
Protecting personal information from unauthorized access or misuse
Increasing storage space
Blocking all advertising

pretest.explanation: Data privacy is about controlling who can access, use, or misuse your personal information.

pretest.text: Should an app always be granted every permission it requests?

choices.text: No — only permissions the app actually needs for its function
Yes, if it is a popular app
Only on new phones
Yes, apps need full access to work

pretest.explanation: Many apps request more access than they need — granting only what is necessary limits data exposure.

pretest.text: What is a risk of oversharing personal details on social media?

There is no real risk
It can give attackers information useful for scams or impersonation
It uses more phone storage

pretest.text: Can data collected by a free app ever be sold to other companies?

Only for banking apps

Periodically reviewing app permissions and privacy settings

Using the same password for every account

The current weather forecast in your city
A public library open hours schedule
Your favorite movie genre

Precise GPS location coordinates and timestamp information

pretest.text: What is the main function of third-party tracking cookies across multiple websites?

choices.text: Encrypting your computer hard drive
Storing the website color scheme
Constructing detailed behavioral profiles of your browsing habits across different web domains
Speeding up internet connection bandwidth

pretest.explanation: Third-party tracking cookies follow users across diverse websites to aggregate personal interests and consumer profiles.

quiz.text: Why should a flashlight app not need access to your contacts?

choices.text: It needs contacts to work properly
That permission has no legitimate connection to its function
All apps need contacts access
It improves battery life

quiz.explanation: A flashlight app has no legitimate reason to need your contacts — that request goes beyond the app's actual function.

quiz.text: What is a risk of posting travel dates and your address publicly?

choices.text: It signals when your home may be empty
It uses too much data
It slows down your phone
It violates copyright

quiz.explanation: Combining public travel details with an address can indicate exactly when a home is unoccupied.

quiz.text: What should you do with app permission requests that seem unnecessary?

choices.text: Always accept them
Deny them and see if the app still works
Uninstall the app immediately without checking
Ignore the prompt

quiz.explanation: Only granting permissions an app actually needs limits what data it can collect.

quiz.text: What is one benefit of requesting data deletion from unused accounts?

choices.text: It speeds up the app
It limits what could be exposed in a future breach
It is required every month
It changes your password automatically

quiz.explanation: Removing data from accounts you no longer use limits what a future breach could expose.

quiz.text: Why is limiting your audience when sharing photos a good privacy habit?

choices.text: It reduces what a stranger can learn and act on
It makes photos load faster
It is required by most platforms
It improves photo quality

quiz.explanation: Limiting who can see personal photos and their timing reduces what an unknown viewer can learn and act on.

choices.text: Grant all permissions so the calculator can run at maximum performance
Deny the permissions because a calculator has no genuine need for camera or contact data

quiz.explanation: Adhering to the principle of least privilege means refusing permissions that bear no connection to the core function of the app.

quiz.text: What sensitive information can EXIF metadata embedded in photos accidentally reveal?

choices.text: The exact GPS coordinates of where the picture was taken and the exact date and time
The private Wi-Fi network key where the picture was captured
